segments.translation: It was pretty good back then. Based on what I know that I say it was good back then. People were important to one another, enjoyed [one] another, had humorous conversations. But, as time went on, I began to see it change. The value of things made it hard for us—on the price of things, about money. But as far as the mind and the way of thinking, it was better than the value of anything. But, nowadays, the price of things is really hard on us. The reason is people have moved from the way that they believed. And how man should walk here on this earth, with his own strength, and gather good to prosper. The way I see it, their own eyes have blinded them, Charlie. That’s what I see. As well as belief—they don’t believe anymore. They have nothing to do with the way we did things in the past. As far as I know, it is going to go back to that. Two different things are going to happen. I tell people, “It’s just going to be the way we are living now.” And, the other thing, is it going to be the way it was? And the way a person wants to be, and wants to live, he will choose. It will be good, or it will be sad. And it is sad, like I am saying, the things that are happening in the world is blinding the people. They are drawn to that. And the Lord that we have been provided is very joyful they are letting go of that. They feel like there is no truth. Quickly, they will think something else. That was the way it was. We were fishing, this One sitting here, I believe you know, too? But I don’t know if he knows where this is at? Do you know where Hickory Hollow is? Where the cemetery is? ‘Hickory Van Hollow’ they call it. Where the cemetery is, on the edge of the field, on this side, is where we used to live. In 1960 we had a drought. Charlie, where I am saying, I traveled that far through this field to the big Sallisaw Creek. A man named Man Hitter owned those fields. I would go across there with two buckets. There was a well there, on the creek. But in the creek there was no water—it was dry. That’s what happened. Then I done as much as could do, bending about to bring them water before it got hot. That’s the way it was when I grew up. And they washed... Back then washers did not exist. They call them ‘washing machine’ in English, they didn’t exist then. That far in the hollow, we were coming from there. They had one of those big things you put water in. They would take it that far to the big creek. I was telling this One, we are the same age, there is a rock there that has a groove in it. A hard rock there. I saw Mom for the first time, doing this. I was watching her I said, “Mom why are you beating those rocks? You are going to put holes in there.” I told her—we probably had one change of clothes. There was a rock there this big, ’kinda round. We were putting water in there for her, and she would put them [clothes] in there. And for soap—she was using that hard soap, all that. And, when she got enough, she pound them with the rocks. That’s when I thought she was going to put holes in our clothes. And, then we would help wring them out, just there on the creek, we hung clothes on the branches. While the clothes were drying we would look for our food. Crawdads, fish, and we would stick our hands under rocks. Yeah, we would just cook right there. Sometimes they would have potatoes. About this time there would be a garden, things like that, as well as onion. They would have a pan in the fire. They would boil crawdads in there. They would fry those crawdads. When they would get done, and when they were almost done, they would put the potatoes and onions, and those ‘kian’ they call them. Them elders always had those kian, hot peppers. They would cut those up. That was a good soup to drink. And crawdads fried real soft. Yeah that’s the way it was. And then, late in the evening, almost sundown, we would pack our clothes back to wear all the way back. That is the way it was back then. And, nowadays, they have washers and driers. I know they would, still won’t, feel like doing it [the laundry]—that’s the way it is. In the winter, we would cut wood to build a fire.

segments.translation: Charlie—that hill by the house, that goes up towards arches, up the hill? I have got some hogs in a pen. There were some tsukvnoni trees there, ’long time ago. I remember it was in the year ’58. It was hot in the month of August. I don’t know if you remember, or y’all remember Wal Sul? Wal Sul was his name. That what was the name of that boy, that his house burned down, in Bunch? Harold Wayne, where Harold Wayne Asbill lives. Right about there. It was just laying right there. They used to call them ‘caboose.’ He had one like that there. And he lived in it, that Wal Sul—a stove for winter, and stove to cook with, he had them both. He wanted some wood, he ordered from my dad and grandpa. Where I am, tell you, these trees were those tsukvnoni—one rick [4' x 8' wood stack] for the cook stove, and one rick for the wood stove. We cut wood there, in the heat. They call it ‘crosscut saw’ in English. We were using one like that—it had long teeth and wooden handles on both sides. Someone would stand on this side, and the other on that side. They would work together. Me and my brothers would have difficulties when we would cut wood. Someone... because if someone is pushing down, it’s heavy to pull. It was then we would get into arguments. “Get off of it.” Really. At this time, I’m saying his name was Fish—Andrew Glass. Fish—y’all probably knew him. He had some mules and a wagon, he hauled that wood for us. I felt really good, I was glad, it was good. I felt like I was just playing around, I didn’t feel like they were working me hard. I didn’t think, “Why do I have to work?” Like I said, it felt like I was just playing around. In the evening, it was the same. I still feel the same way, Michael, I still feel the same way. I feel good, yeah.
That’s good.

segments.translation: We loaded them up. First it was for the cook stove. And, Charlie if you remember—horse pulled wagon, where they hook up was all sticking out in the back. Would get up on there, and sit and look around. We delivered that wood. He gave them half—50 cents, yeah, half. Fifty cents a rick of cook stove wood, and, for the wood stove, a quarter [25 cents]. And that’s what it was in 1958. That’s the way it was back then. Also, you could cut wood wherever. Nobody would say nothing. Nobody would come and see you. Also, there were not fences anywhere, back then, where the woods are. It wasn’t woods—that’s what I tell my family, gah-lee, when they speak in English they say ‘jungle’—that’s the way it is there, Charlie. If you remember, maybe you haven’t been there? South Bunch, across the railroad tracks, by the house, where that big field is? There was a big house there, and just over here was a huge horse barn. We came there about that time, there in Hickory Van Hollow. We just went there. I used to think we traveled a long ways. I used to think we went a long ways, when we moved. It was close by. There, where I am talking about, I would help my dad make fence posts and railroad ties. We would cut them down, so he could make posts and ties. I tell my family I have grown up. Boy, I worked hard since I was six years old. I was six years old, Charlie—I started then. But that’s the way it was then. A child wasn’t going to lay down somewhere, or be sitting somewhere, in the cold, in the heat. Where Charlie lives, we would be that far [away] on that mountain, we would come from out of that hollow. We would leave there at four in the morning. There, past where y’all live, in that corner where that gate is, we would be walking right there. It would turn daylight. We would get there—it is called ‘Two Springs.’ On the other ridge, that’s where it was. We would be coming back in the evening. We would get back to the hollow around nine the next morning. The same thing, that’s the way it was back then. That’s the kind of things he would do. He [Dad] bought that land where we live now. He paid it off, he borrowed money from the Cherokee Nation.

segments.translation: Back then all of our relatives were just, like, in a group there. All us. But there was some that lived at Greasy, that way, when we still lived in Hickory Van Hollow. As well as South Bunch. People from that far. We were all together. It was almost like that all the time, Charlie. We didn’t see one another every now and then. There, everywhere on Maxwell Mountain, we would see each other all the time. That’s the way it was. But, nowadays, we live close to each other, we barely see each other. We live just next to each other, but we won’t see each other until way then.

segments.translation: Me, I was maybe around eight years old. They opened it up. A soldier, clothes, a soldier stepped down. I thought he was the one that helps people. I was watching him. Everyone was standing where the door is. They let him out, then they went back that way, and there they let out two dogs—bluetick hound dogs. That was him, Fish, I never knew then. Just the next morning they left. There was a White man that lived on the mountain, Michael, this side—Jim Harris. They went after those horses and wagon, he bought two pairs. We were all up there where Fish grew up. It was late in the afternoon. I heard the sound of chains. I was looking that way, I was at the creek looking for crawdads, I seen somethings—ears they were this long [gestures]. I thought, “What is that?” It was them, those mules and a plow. They had all those things in there, and they were leading two cows for milking, and in the other wagon, ducks, chickens. They had it full in there. It started there, it was probably past noon when they came. When they untied the horses, they hooked up the turning plows. It started then, it didn’t start in the morning, it started then. That’s what I tell these living, that are my family. Boy, I miss them old ones. I miss them, there wasn’t no time for them. It didn’t matter what time. It could be midnight, if they say, “Let’s do it, let’s do it.” They was going to do it. That’s the way them elders were, they were all like that, not just certain ones. They were all like that. The last, where his mom lived down in the hollow, there is a few times that I know of, “Let’s kill a hog, it will just take us a little while. It won’t be long we will be eating fresh meat.” I know of one time, no I know of three times, it was towards midnight we killed a hog. Tsukiyasgi built a fire. He said, “It won’t take long to boil water.” We went and killed it, the water was boiling, then we scraped it, and gutted it. In just a little while we were eating meat and gravy.

segments.translation: Ice, Ice Killer was his name. He was always willing, and his mom was the same way. Like I said, everybody was, this what I’m telling y’all. There, across from where we lived, was that big house there where Fish grew up. You could see all that there was where we used to hoe crops. In that field, all the way to the creek. There wasn’t even a shrub this tall, nowhere. No shrubs, just grass. Sometimes when we go over there I think about things. I see the way it was now it’s growed up—trees are this big. You can’t tell it was a field at one time. That’s the way it is. Where the bridge is, we used to hoe there, this of the railroad tracks, on this was a waterfall. Saws used to live there, too. And, on the other side, that dam wasn’t there yet, Joe and them lived. Over there, this of [unclear] that was where that field started. All the way to the road. I tell people, “Just here where we lived, things were beautiful to look around.” And people go far away—you can just go just around here, in the forest and see beautiful things. I tell them, “The way we were put here on earth, yeah.” Now, here, the next morning, boy Charlie, I was in a hurry for it to turn daylight, so we could start back doing things. It turned daylight, I was sitting on the porch there. I was telling her, “Just yesterday tsawolvdv was making a sound.” I really like to hear a tsawolvdv making a sound. Back then, early in the morning they would make that sound, tsawolvdv. I was listening I was listening to them.

segments.translation: Bluebird, yeah, that’s its name—tsawolvdv. Tsawolvdahi, bluebird. Then Fish’s mom, Tsutliga, they used to call Dad ‘Hue’ short for Houston, “Hue come eat. It’s time to eat.” We would cross there when we got there. There was food on the table she had cooked. I was telling you—they brought chickens, and ducks, and cows, and they had milk there. We ate from them. There was a smokehouse behind this building I’m talking about. Suud used all wood when he built it. And, where he built that smokehouse to keep meat, just there on the side, was a spring. A spring there. They had built a fence that had pickets of wood. That area—they put those ducks in there, and chickens—he had built there, made of wood, years ago. A place to put hay—it was over this way to the north, was that building. They had those cows and chickens in there. We sure made a garden, then it was time to dig potatoes. I was even more happy.

segments.translation: Gah Michael, they stuck that plow in there, where we had potatoes planted. Boy, potatoes were this big [gestures], everything—that’s the way it was. Betty Christie is her name, she lives by the railroad crossing where we call ‘Bunch.’ There was a store there, at the time her dad had that store. And, on the other side, was another man. There they made cornmeal. The people that raised corn, like I said—horse pulled wagons. They would haul them in. They would have cornmeal made there. I forget how much when he would grind it... Maybe he would get five pounds for hisself? That’s the way it was. If you had something I needed, and if I had something and you needed it, they would just give each other—that that’s the way it was. It wasn’t about money, this. I know, if people would do that—like I said, it’s going to go back to that, and it’s going to go back to that—they could still have good lives. It would still be good, if they would help each other out. Helping each other out—that’s what it was. Back then someone would come, he would maybe have a little meat. He would bring it to you, and if you had something to give, you would give him something as he was going home. That’s the way this was. It was really good.

segments.translation: Like I said, we grow crops, they would can stuff, back then. There would be an apple tree on the creek, it would have lots of apples or peaches and plums. We would pick it—we would help peel, and cut up. Some they didn’t can—apples or peaches, they dried them. But, those plums, they would make jelly. I really like that jelly made from plums. We would cut those peaches and apples up, and this table cloth—we would lay those on the roof. We would put, there, the apples and peaches that we cut up. We would all be up there, we would have those sticks—tsuyoni, with leaves. Chasing the flies off all day. Sometimes someone would get off, and someone else would get up there. When evening came they would be dry. Then they would put them in bags, and hang them in the house. And, in the wintertime, they would cook that, or to make pies with. That’s the way it was. They did corn the same way. They would hang them up and dry them. We dried fish out the same way. They would put wood poles with a fork, and put one across. We would hang the fish there. When it came evening the fish were dry. They wouldn’t ruin. Nowadays, you couldn’t do that—the earth is much different now. It has changed, and continues to change. They would wrap those fish, and make soup—baked or fried fish patties. It was good. They would have onion hanging in the smokehouse. They would have onion hanging there, corn, and different things. I built a smokehouse, a place where we could preserve food, I built in the hollow. My dad helped me make the trusses. I cut them 10 foot long. I made it four corners, Charlie. I carried them on my shoulder for a long ways, Mike. I carried them a long ways, I made them. This big... the boys, my brothers, helped me.

segments.text: ᏂᎦᏓ ᎨᎲ ᏔᎵᏚ ᏃᎩᏨ, ᏍᎪᎯ ᎣᏥᏧᏣ ᏔᎵ ᏦᎩᏙ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏎᎾ ᎠᏰᏟᏴ ᎠᏂᏧᏣ Ꮲ ᏯᏁᎯ ᎮᏍᏓ ᏱᎦᏅᏛᏗ ᏙᏚᏙᎥ ᎤᏓᏂᎵᎨ ᎠᏮᎨᏫᏌ ᏚᏙᎥ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏗ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎬᏗᎡ ᎨᎲ Johnny Lee ᏚᏙᎥ ᎮᏍᏓ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏯ ᎠᏩᏓᏂᎵᎨ ᏱᎦ ᎾᎡ ᎤᏓᏂᎵᎨ ᎮᏍᏓ ᎮᏂ ᏰᎯ
segments.transliteration: nigada gehv talidu nogitsv, sgohi otsitsutsa tali tsogido gehv asena ayetliyv anitsutsa tlv yanehi hesda yiganvdvdi dodudov udanilige awvgewisa dudov tsalagi gvdi yonega gvdie gehv Johnny Lee dudov hesda heni aya awadanilige yiga nae udanilige hesda heni yehi
segments.translation: In all there were 12 of us—ten boys, and we have two sisters. But now half the boys have passed away. I don’t remember the oldest one—I forget what his name was in Cherokee. In English his name was Johnny Lee. I am not the oldest one, the oldest one is deceased.
You’re the oldest one now?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s me now—second.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᎠᏬᎯᏳᏒ ᏣᏓᏂᎵᎨ ᎨᎲ. ᎮᏍᏓ ᏯᏩᎾᏖ ᏐᎢ ᎡᎲ
segments.transliteration: awohiyusv tsadanilige gehv. hesda yawanate soi ehv
segments.translation: I thought you were the oldest, I didn’t know there was another that lived.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: yeah, ᏐᎢ ᎮᏂ ᎡᎲ ᏏᏅ ᎠᏯ ᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: yeah, soi heni ehv sinv aya gehv
segments.translation: Yeah, there was another, other than me.
How long did he live?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: They said maybe about eight months.
Eight months.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: ᎾᎯᏳ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᎫᏍᏓ ᏳᎾᎵᏍᏓᏁᎵ ᏁᎲᎾ ᏓᏂᏲᎱᏍᎨ ᎧᏂᎩᏓ ᎫᏍᏓ. ᏍᎫ ᎠᏂᏲᏁᎦ ᎤᎾᎵᏨ ᎨᎮ Ꮩ ᏄᎾᎵᏍᏓᏁᎲ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ. ᏙᎯ ᎬᏰᏙ ᎠᏂᏟᏅᏅ ᎠᏂᏲᎱᏍᎨ ᏓᏂᏲᎱᏍᎨ. ᏳᏍᏕ ᎢᎩᏠᎢᏴ ᎢᏗᏴᏫᏯ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎤᏂᏩᏛᎲ ᏧᏩᏚᏃ Ꭱ ᏂᏚᏅᏁᎮ ᎤᎿᎾ ᏚᏂᏢᎨ ᏧᏩᏚᏃ ᏍᎩᎿᏅ ᎬᏂᎨ Ꮕ ᎠᏃᎮᎮ ᏍᎩᎿᏅ ᎩᎶᏫᏴᏅ ᏱᎪᏓ ᏲᏭᏢᎦ ᎨᎮ ᎠᎾᏗᎲ Ꮟ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏍᎩ ᏄᏍᏓ. ᎡᎵ ᎯᎸᏍᏄᏒ ᎬᏳᏓᎴᏅᏗ ᏍᏈᏍᏕ ᏴᏫ ᏍᎩ ᏄᎾᎵᏍᏓᏁ ᏃᏩ ᏥᎦ. ᏧᎾᏛᏂᏅ Ꭱ ᏍᎩ ᏄᎾᎵᏍᏓᏁ ᎦᏕᎳᎣᏍᎦ ᎮᏂ ᎤᎾᎡ ᏳᏭᎯᎶᎦ ᏴᏩ ᎬᏬᎮᎸ ᎨᎲ. ᎢᎦᏓ ᎤᏂᏔᏝᏬᏒᏓ ᎾᏅᎵᏍᏗ ᎢᎦᏓ Ꮕ ᏣᏓ ᎧᏂᎩᏓ ᏣᏓ ᎠᎵᏟᏖᏟᏗ ᎢᎦᏗᏅ ᎤᏂᏢᏗᏭ ᏱᎦ ᏳᎾᏚᎵ ᎥᏍᎨ ᏄᏍᏓ ᏴᏫ ᎬᏂᎨ Ꭱ ᎤᏍᎦᏎᏗ ᎤᏪᎲ ᎥᏬᎮᎸᎡ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᎯᏅ ᏍᎫ ᏅᏬᏘ ᎯᎢ ᎠᏟᏅᏬᏙᏗ ᏙᎯ ᏳᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗ ᏴᏫ ᎾᎯᏳ Ꭱ ᏍᎨ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎯᏃ ᎤᎿᎾ Ꮎ ᏗᏂᏠᏫ ᎠᏁᎲ Leon, Leo ᎢᎾ ᏚᎾᏙᎥ. ᏃᏭᏅ Susie ᎣᎩᏙ ᎤᎾ ᎠᏰᏟ ᎡᎯ ᎠᏧᏣ ᏢᏰᎯ ᏍᎫ. SᎫ ᏁᎲᎾ ᏄᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᏃᏭᏅ Susie, Dorothy ᎠᏁᎲ ᏏᏭ Ꮠ ᎠᏰᏟ ᎡᎯ ᎠᏧᏣ ᏍᎫ Ꮲ ᏰᎭ ᎤᎿᏃ Tex, Jimmy Waite, Billy Ꮓ ᎣᏂ yeah ᏍᎨᎾ ᏄᏍᏓ yeah
segments.transliteration: nahiyu heni tsigehv diniyotli gusda yunalisdaneli nehvna daniyohusge kanigida gusda. sgu aniyonega unalitsv gehe do nunalisdanehv diniyotli. dohi gvyedo anitlinvnv aniyohusge daniyohusge. yusde igitloiyv idiyvwiya yusdi uniwadvhv tsuwaduno e nidunvnehe uhnana dunitlvge tsuwaduno sgihnanv gvnige nv anohehe sgihnanv gilowiyvnv yigoda yowutlvga gehe anadihv si gohiyv tsiga sgi nusda. eli hilvsnusv gvyudalenvdi squisde yvwi sgi nunalisdane nowa tsiga. tsunadvninv e sgi nunalisdane gadelaosga heni unae yuwuhiloga yvwa gvwohelv gehv. igada unitatlawosvda nanvlisdi igada nv tsada kanigida tsada alitlitetlidi igadinv unitlvdiwu yiga yunaduli vsge nusda yvwi gvnige e usgasedi uwehv vwohelve tsigehv ehinv sgu nvwoti hii atlinvwododi dohi yunigalisdi yvwi nahiyu e sge nusda nahiyu tsigehv hino uhnana na dinitlowi anehv Leon, Leo ina dunadov. nowunv Susie ogido una ayetli ehi atsutsa tlvyehi sgu. Sgu nehvna nulisdvnv nowunv Susie, Dorothy anehv siwu so ayetli ehi atsutsa sgu tlv yeha uhnano Tex, Jimmy Waite, Billy no oni yeah sgena nusda yeah
segments.translation: Back then, children that didn’t seem like there was anything wrong with them just passed away. Nothing wrong. The White people couldn’t even figure it out—what was wrong with the children. They would be OK, but they would die in their sleep. What they found in us-that-are-related—natives; it was in the nerves—there was a sickness in the nerves they called ‘black.’ It would cover you pretty quick. It’s still that way, nowadays. It started a while back. Many people have that—adults, it’s happening to adults. I can see it happening, a person will be driven to that. I have been told some will develop a temper, and some won’t be able to move. Some will just want to sleep. That is the way a person will be, if they have that strongly within them. I have been told there is a medicine that exist to heal one’s self—a person can become well. Back then, that’s the way it was. And, now, the twins-that-were-living, their names were Leon and Leo. And then Susie, our sister, and, the boy-that-was-between-them ain’t alive, he passed away. And, then, between Susie and Dorothy, that One passed away, too. And then there is Tex, Jimmy, Watie, and Billy—the last. Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᎮᎴ, ᎬᏯᏛᏓᏍᏛᏭ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎠᎩᏰᎸ ᎡᏝᏪ ᎠᏬᏢ
segments.transliteration: hele, gvyadvdasdvwu osda agiyelv etlawe awotlv
segments.translation: I was just sitting here, enjoying listening to you.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: Sitting there, quiet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᎿᎾᎭ ᏍᎩᏃᎯᏌ ᏍᏗ ᏳᏍᏓ ᎢᏥᏫᏒᏍᎬ ᎠᏯᏅ ᎤᏟ ᏱᎦ ᎠᏩᏚᎵᎲ Ꮩ ᎢᏣᏛᏁᎮ ᏕᏥᏍᏆᏂᎪᏗᎮ ᏄᎾ
segments.transliteration: hnanaha sginohisa sdi yusda itsiwisvsgv ayanv utli yiga awadulihv do itsadvnehe detsisquanigodihe nuna
segments.translation: Tell us a little bit about what y’all planted. I would really like to know how y’all preserved the potatoes.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: yeah, Ꮎ ᏥᏓᏥᏃᎮᏟᏒ Ꮎ ᏧᎦᎩᏠᏩ ᏐᎢ Ꮎ ᎣᏥᏍᏆᏂᎪᏗᎲ ᎠᎵᏍᏓᏴᏗ ᏥᎬᏓ ok. ᏃᏩ Ꮎ ᏄᎾ see ᏌᏭ ᎮᏂ ᎢᎦ ᏗᎦᎴᏍᏓ ᏄᎾ July ᎧᎸ. ᎤᎾ ᏱᏭᏓᏬᎯᎸᏓ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᎾᎪᏍᎪ Ꭱ ᏯᎾᎴᎾ ᏍᎫ ᎦᏳᎳ ᏱᏗᏣᎴᏌ ᏳᏩᎾᎪ ᎤᏪ ᎥᏍᎨ ᏄᏍᏗᏓᏂ. ᎯᎿᎾ Ꮟ ᏥᎦᏓᏅᏖᏭ ᎠᏣᏗᏅ ᏍᎫ ᏌᏭ ᎢᎦ ᏍᎫ July ᎧᎳ ᎠᏂᎾᎷᏍᎨ ᎠᏣᏓ ᎦᏚᏌ ᎠᎦᏓ ᎾᎯᏳ Ꭱ ᎠᎯᏓ ᏗᎯᏍᏗ ᎾᏢ ᎤᏅᏬᏓ ᏥᎨᎰ ᎤᏅᏬᏙ ᎤᎾ ᎮᏂ ᏣᏓ ᏓᏂᏍᏆᏨᏂᎲ ᎤᎾ ᎬᏗᏟᏙᎲ ᎨᎲ ᏙᏯ ᏫᏗᎬᏓᎡᎬ yeah ᏌᏭ ᎢᎦ ᏢᏅᏍᎫ all day I ᏱᎦ ᎭᏯᏩᏔ hour, hour and a half ᏍᎫᏢ ᏱᎪᎯᏓ ᏍᎩ ᎿᏅᏛᏁ ᎠᏣᏓ ᎥᏍᎨ ᏳᏍᏓ ᎤᎾᏅᏛ ᎠᏂᎬᏴᎳ ᎾᎯᏳᏅ ᎣᏤᎪ charlie ᎯᎿᎾ ᏄᎾ ᎾᎡᎿ, ᎢᏣᏗᏛ ᏳᏍᏓ ᎨᎲ ᎧᏁᏍᎦᏬ
segments.transliteration: yeah, na tsidatsinohetlisv na tsugagitlowa soi na otsisquanigodihv alisdayvdi tsigvda ok. nowa na nuna see sawu heni iga digalesda nuna July kalv. una yiwudawohilvda sgina anagosgo e yanalena sgu gayula yiditsalesa yuwanago uwe vsge nusdidani. hihnana si tsigadanvtewu atsadinv sgu sawu iga sgu July kala aninalusge atsada gadusa agada nahiyu e ahida dihisdi natlv unvwoda tsigeho unvwodo una heni tsada danisquatsvnihv una gvditlidohv gehv doya widigvdaegv yeah sawu iga tlvnvsgu all day I yiga hayawata hour, hour and a half sgutlv yigohida sgi hnanvdvne atsada vsge yusda unanvdv anigvyvla nahiyunv otsego charlie hihnana nuna naehna, itsadidv yusda gehv kanesgawo
segments.translation: I was going to talk about that before you asked me. We were, I said we preserved food. OK, you see, you can only dig potatoes once in the month of July. If it goes beyond that, they will start to rot. Even if you get them out, they will just rot. That is the way it is. While I’m still thinking about this, fish go upstream one day out of the month of July. [They swim] uphill at that time. It is easy to kill fish where it’s shallow real shallow, there. They will be going back and forth. I would be running around, throwing them out of the water. Yeah, one day. And it ain’t all day. I don’t know, it’s for an hour or an hour and half—just that long. That’s what the fish do. That’s the kind of things the elders know. That’s when we go. Charlie, these potatoes—do y’all what ‘kvnesgvwo’ is?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t. Just hay.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: OK, write it down, write it down: Kvnesgvwo.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: ᎥᏍᎩᎾ ᏣᏅᏔ ᏗᏕᎬ ᏗᏝ Ꮕ ᏠᎨᏌ ᏣᏛᏍᎦ, ᎨᏯᏔ ᏛᎮ ᏱᏛᏗ ᏓᎭ ᎦᏄᎸ
segments.transliteration: vsgina tsanvta didegv ditla nv tlogesa tsadvsga, geyata dvhe yidvdi daha ganulv
segments.translation: You know, where we come from, that grows in the field. I guess we can say it’s ‘wild grass.’

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: ᎥᏍᎩᎡ ᏦᏥᎦᎵᏍᎬ ᏃᏭᏅ ᏥᏥᏰᏍᏛᏍᎬ ᎯᎢ ᏢᏳᏅᏪᏓ ᏥᏃᏨᏁᎲ ᎯᎢ ᏳᎭᎨᏓ Ꮎ ᏄᎾ ᏦᎩᏗ. ᏃᏍᎩ ᏱᏃᎬᏁᎶᏂ ᎯᎢ ᏱᎦ ᏄᎾ ᏙᎩᎲ ᏃᎴ ᏐᎢ ᏥᏥᏰᏍᏛᏍᎬ Ꮓ ᏧᎦᏂᏕᏂ ᏱᎦ ᎠᎴ ᏚᏯ ᏱᎦ ᏍᎩᎿᎾ ᎠᏛᏍᎦ. ᎥᏍᎨ ᏥᏃᏨᏁᎲ ᎤᎵᎪᎲᏍᏓᏅ ᏣᏓ ᏃᏭᏅ ᎣᎩᎦᏓᏙᏛᏅ ᎠᏫᏒᏅ ᎤᏠᏯ ᏏᏭ ᎩᎳ ᎪᎩ ᏗᏝ Ꮓ ᏥᎨᏐ ᎡᎵᏏ Ꮕ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᏂᎬᏴᎵ ᏣᏁᎲ ᎡᏥ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᎾ ᏫᎾᏅᏕᏍᎪ ᎨᎲ ᏄᎾ ᏱᎦ ᎯᎠᏢ ᎾᏅᏛᎣ ᎢᏤ ᎠᏅᏂᏍᏗᎰ ᏓᏆᏌᏂ ᎤᏠᏱ. Yeah ᏍᎩᎡ ᏥᏄᏍᏛ ᎯᎾᎿ
segments.transliteration: vsgie tsotsigalisgv nowunv tsitsiyesdvsgv hii tlvyunvweda tsinotsvnehv hii yuhageda na nuna tsogidi. nosgi yinogvneloni hii yiga nuna dogihv nole soi tsitsiyesdvsgv no tsuganideni yiga ale duya yiga sgihnana advsga. vsge tsinotsvnehv uligohvsdanv tsada nowunv ogigadadodvnv awisvnv utloya siwu gila gogi ditla no tsigeso elisi nv tsigehv anigvyvli tsanehv etsi tsigehv una winanvdesgo gehv nuna yiga hiatlv nanvdvo itse anvnisdiho daquasani utloyi. Yeah sgie tsinusdv hinahna
segments.translation: We used to cut that. Then we would lay it down and make it about this thick [gestures] where we put the potatoes. Then, when we did that, we would put another layer on top. Then, like cabbage, and beans, things that grow—that’s how we used to do it. And, in the fall, what we had harvested from the garden, we did the same. [In] the spring... spring, my grandmother, when the elders were alive, or Mom—that’s where they would get from. The potatoes, new potatoes, they would cook, it turnup the same way. Yeah, that’s the way this was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That ‘kvnesgvwo’ you are talking about—it was a... a grass?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: Yeah, it was grass.

segments.text: ᏙᏅ ᎤᏍᏓ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎬᏗ ᏴᏓ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎧᏁᏍᎦᏬ?
segments.transliteration: donv usda yonega gvdi yvda sgina kanesgawo?
segments.translation: What’s it name in English, kvnesgvwo?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: Charlie Ꮩ ᎤᏍᏓ ᏚᏙ ᏍᎩᎾ prairie grass Ꮝ?
segments.transliteration: Charlie do usda dudo sgina prairie grass s?
segments.translation: Charlie, what is the name of that? Prairie grass, that’s it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what I was going to say.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: yeah, ᏍᎩᏛ ᎨᎵ prairie grass yeah ᎧᏁᏍᎦᏬ
segments.transliteration: yeah, sgidv geli prairie grass yeah kanesgawo
segments.translation: I think so—prairie grass, kvnesgvwo.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You said those potatoes could make it through the winter?

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.text: ᎪᎵ ᎠᏂᎦᏛᎴᏍᎬ charlie ᏂᎦᏓ ᎪᎳ ᎠᏂᎦᏛᎴᏍᎬ
segments.transliteration: goli anigadvlesgv charlie nigada gola anigadvlesgv
segments.translation: They would make it through the winter, Charlie. All winter, they would make it through.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᏄᏰᏟᏛ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎬᏯᏛᎭ ᎢᎦᏓ ᎬᎩᏃᏎᎲ. ᎡᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᏍᎪᏍᎬ ᎦᏙ ᎠᎾᏗᎲ ᎮᏂ ᎤᎿᏅ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏳᏍᏓ ᎧᏁᏍᎦᏬ ᏥᏃᎮ ᎤᏠᏯ ᎿᏅᏁᎮ
segments.transliteration: nuyetlidv heni tsigvyadvha igada gvginosehv. edoda tsigehv asgosgv gado anadihv heni uhnanv sgina yusda kanesgawo tsinohe utloya hnanvnehe
segments.translation: The reason I was asking you: some were telling me that their dad would dig a hole in the ground. And, there they put that ‘kvnesgvwo,’ what you are talking about, and did the same.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: They would do the same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᏞᏲ ᏯᎾᏗᎮ ᎧᏁᏍᎦᏬ ᎨᎲᏲ ᏲᏍᎩᏂ ᏲᏍᎩᏂ ᎤᏅᏌ ᎧᏁᏍᎦ ᎠᎾᏗᎲ
segments.transliteration: tleyo yanadihe kanesgawo gehvyo yosgini yosgini unvsa kanesga anadihv
segments.translation: They didn’t say it was prairie grass, but, they said it was hay.

segments.speaker: bobby-pettit
segments.translation: Hay—that would be it though, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.text: ᎤᎾ ᏙᏥᏢᏍᎬ ᏃᏭ ᎣᏧᏢᏍᎬ ᎠᎾᏗᎲ ᎮᏂ
segments.transliteration: una dotsitlvsgv nowu otsutlvsgv anadihv heni
segments.translation: They said they would put them in there, and cover it up.

segments.translation: Really, really Charlie, that. I used to help Mom make it. We would start early in the morning. We had a kettle—she would say, “Put four gallons of water.” I would put that much water, and I would build the fire, and then, back then like I said—money wasn’t nothing. We melt the pig fat, we would save it—[in] that four-pound bucket. She would put in that much grease and burn it [the wood]—they would use blackjack or hickory [ash]. They said it was the best [to make soap]. They would mix that, and, like I said, I would build the fire. It would boil and boil. Around about noon, I remember, it would get heavy, even more. I would stir it. When it got that far, “That’s enough boy. Just let that fire go out. Let it go out.” Then we would cover it up with something. She would wait ’till the next morning. She would take a pan and knife, [pour the mixture in], and it would harden. Then you would use a knife [to cut the soap into bars]. Yeah, that’s what it would be—to wash with, and to clean up with. It was like that. And also, I’m going to say something, back then if something bit you, they would use that [lye soap]. That will heal you too. What you’re saying—that soap. Yeah, like a mosquito or tick—something like that. Yeah, that will kill all of that. They knew quite a bit those elders-that-were-living. That’s what they used to do, that. segments.translation: Blackjack nodi—this what we are talking about. Now that that we have harvested everything that grew, the very best and biggest seed—they would choose the biggest. A long time ago, what we call plastic—that did not exist. It was metal. We would put it [nodi] in there, then, the year—next spring; they would plant. That... that’s the way it was. And bugs can get in there, even flour bugs can get in there, everything. Bugs will tear up, I don’t know where they come from—they used to use soft tobacco [chewing tobacco] it was called ‘Honest.’ Old women would put it in their mouth.
